verdicts.why: Names a religious order's garment plainly; nothing in the word approves or disparages the wearer.
A plain term for riding dress; it identifies the clothing and takes no side on it.
Technical botanical and crystallographic term for growth form, purely descriptive.
A technical name for a hardware component; no attitude rides on the word.
Names a field of study; it describes a discipline without judging it.
It reports that the subject found something wrong or unacceptable, but the word itself is the plain neighbour of spurn or dismiss and carries no attitude of the speaker's.
A plain, even administrative, term for refusing admission; blackball or spurn would carry the contempt, reject does not.
Medical term for an immune response to a transplant; the body is not being judged.
In the sense of a kind or manner (a style of building, a style of writing) the word classifies without praising; the approval in 'she has style' belongs to a different sense.
Names the prevailing taste of a period; whether something is in or out of it is a fact the word reports, not an attitude the word carries.
House style is a set of editorial conventions; a neutral technical term.
Names a writing instrument, a plain object noun.
Botanical anatomy term; purely descriptive.
Zoological anatomy term for a bristle-like process; purely descriptive.
Names two people who are together; it neither blesses nor mocks the pairing, unlike lovebirds or item.
A physics term for paired opposing forces; no attitude possible.
In the sense of identifying a specimen or species it is a neutral act of classification; the flattering 'distinguished' of the sentences is a different sense.
Plain verb for separating into parts; splitting a heart or an estate is described, not judged.
Plain verb for parting or coming apart; carries no attitude toward what parts.
Arithmetic operation; wholly neutral.
Names combustion itself; the plainest possible word for it.
A hearth or cooking fire is named plainly; warmth in the referent is not warmth in the word.
Military term for shooting; a bad referent named in a plain word, not a loaded word.
In 'under fire' or 'draw fire' the word means criticism that is intense and hostile; that intensity is its meaning, and the speaker takes no side on whether the criticism is deserved.
In 'go through the fire' the word means a severe ordeal; strong meaning, but no attitude toward the person tried beyond the severity itself.
